title: The Extracellular Matrix is Potentially a Key Regulator in Long COVID, Hypermobility Disorders, and Related Conditions
content: Long coronavirus disease (long COVID) and hypermobility disorders (e.g., hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) often share comorbidities, including mast cell activation syndrome, small fiber neuropathy, and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome. The relationship between long COVID and hypermobility disorders, as well as the extracellular matrix (ECM), has been reported, with evidence suggesting that ECM alterations may underlie these associations. The current hypothesis posits that ECM alterations may become partly self-perpetuating, with the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 spike protein as a possible initial trigger. The proposed mechanism involves interactions among the spike protein, integrins, latent transforming growth factor β, mast cells, interleukin-6, and matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9). Possible feedback loops, such as those between latent transforming growth factor β and a stiffened ECM, increased sympathetic activity and a pro-inflammatory state, insulin resistance and a pro-inflammatory state, inflammation and mast cell migration, and increased blood–brain barrier permeability via MMP-9 and inflammation, are highlighted. The impact of the modified ECM on the nervous system, as described through PIEZO and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, is also discussed, alongside evidence for increased differentiation of T-helper 17 cells and their potentially disruptive effects on efferocytosis. This new hypothesis may have important implications for clinical practice and future research.
